overview: West Germany was the common Cold War name for the Federal Republic of Germany, founded in 1949 in the western occupation zones. Its Basic Law and elected parliament endured after 1990. In its early decades, families faced severe housing shortages; later growth brought new homes, refrigerators and washing machines to many. Workers recruited from abroad and their children became part of the country, while women pressed against unequal roles and students challenged schools and authority. West Germany as a separate map label ended with reunification in 1990, but the Federal Republic continued. The imported map covers only 1960 to 1994.

periods.title: Republic and rebuilding
periods.summary: The Basic Law and Bundestag framed the new democracy while subsidized homes slowly eased postwar crowding.

periods.title: Growth and social change
periods.summary: Appliances and jobs spread, but the boom depended on many migrant workers and prompted debate about family roles and education.

periods.title: Migration, reform and division
periods.summary: Recruitment stopped in 1973, many workers stayed and brought relatives, and the Federal Republic remained divided from the GDR until 1990.

periods.title: Federal Republic continues
periods.summary: The GDR joined the Federal Republic; the Cold War label West Germany faded, while its constitutional and parliamentary state continued.

items.text: The Federal Republic began in 1949. Voters chose Bundestag representatives in free elections, unlike the GDR’s controlled Volkskammer before 1990. West Berlin had a special status and did not hold the same Bundestag elections.
The Basic Law begins “Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar,” or “Human dignity is inviolable.” That small written German sample helped set the republic’s legal direction after Nazi rule.

Students protested in the 1960s over crowded universities, education reform and old ideas about authority. The debates showed that democratic life includes arguments in classrooms and streets, not just votes on election day.

The GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. Thus “West Germany” ended as the name for one half of a divided country, but the Federal Republic’s Basic Law and elected institutions continued.

In 1949 the western republic had far more households than available dwellings. A 1950 survey found roughly three households for every two homes, and only about half had a cooking place to themselves. Privacy, kitchens and toilets mattered as much as the national flag.
The 1950 housing law supported affordable construction. More than five million homes were built with public help by 1960, although early subsidized flats were small and allocated according to need.

By 1965, refrigerators and washing machines had reached most households; supermarkets and television ads changed shopping. The “economic miracle” was built by workers and did not mean everyone could buy everything at once.

West Germany’s statutory health insurance continued an older system and expanded during the republic. The practical family question was whether a sick child could see a doctor without paying the whole bill at the door; insurance rules helped answer it.
The 1950s celebrated a mother-at-home ideal, but more married women took paid work. Women often received less pay for the same work; legal equality and everyday equality moved at different speeds.

From 1955 to 1973 the government recruited workers from Italy, Turkey, Spain and six other countries. Many lived in strict dormitories at first. After recruitment stopped, many stayed and brought families: the supposedly temporary “guest” had children, neighbors and a long future.

West German education came under fire in the 1960s for unequal opportunities and overcrowded universities. Pupils did not all receive the same route to higher study; reformers argued over who school was really for.

Industrial growth helped many households buy more, but employers’ profits rose faster than wages at points and workers fought over pay and hours. A new fridge did not settle arguments about who worked, earned and cooked.

For families with relatives in East Germany, the 1961 Berlin Wall turned an ordinary visit into a political problem. The two state cards describe different daily lives, but many family stories crossed the divide.

ending.text: West Germany as a Cold War half-country label ended when the GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The Federal Republic itself continued with its Basic Law and elected parliament; millions of East and West residents and migrant families entered this new chapter together. The imported 1994 endpoint is not a second unification.
